items.t: One year later, Tesla and Musk still don’t have a good definition of ‘abundance’
items.d: The CEO promised to get more specific about his vision. But the details are still absent.
items.fullText: On September 1, 2025, Elon Musk laid out his fourth “ Master Plan ” for Tesla, which was immediately criticized by some of his most ardent fans for being generic . Musk agreed and promised to add more specifics. They never came. But that hasn’t stopped Musk and other Tesla executives from spending much of the past year promising that the company’s many futuristic efforts — robotaxis, robots, AI — are all part of a grander machine that will create an era of “amazing abundance.” What that means, more than a year later, is still tricky to pin down. The topline promises of the plan have remained big and bawdy even as its tagline has changed from sustainable abundance — a clearer connection to the company’s former mission — to the “amazing abundance” slogan, which Musk chose because it was “more joyful.” Musk has talked about a far-flung future where robots and AI do surgery and increase access to medical care. He has said the proliferation of AI and robotics means that “everyone can have a penthouse if they want.” He (virtually) shouted “Amazing abundance for all!” in a quote-tweet of a post from Midjourney founder David Holz, who had claimed 5 million humanoid robots could “build Manhattan in ~6 months.” In July, Musk told Economist editor-in-chief Zanny Minton Beddoes that amazing abundance means “anyone can have anything they can think of.” He also mentioned on Joe Rogan’s podcast late last year that “sustainable abundance” would mean “we haven’t destroyed nature” or “paved the rainforest” and we still “have the national parks,” despite supporting two politicians — Donald Trump and Jair Bolsonaro — who have actively worked against those goals. items.fullText: AI Security Is an Engineering Problem — How to Solve It at Every Layer of the Agent Stack Open research, controls across the agent stack and continuous testing help defenders build and operate more secure AI systems. September 21, 2026 by Saša Zdjelar 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! AI security is an engineering problem. That means defined security requirements, enforceable controls, named owners and evidence that protections work. As AI becomes more capable, the industry must accelerate security engineering, broaden access to defensive tools and share what works faster. Technology Changes, Security Fundamentals Endure The internet and cloud computing changed how software operates, while core security responsibilities endured: establish identity, control access, limit exposure and verify that protections work. AI agents introduce new capabilities — reasoning , using tools and adapting actions based on the data they encounter. Those capabilities require applying established principles to new operating conditions. This pace creates pressure. Organizations want the productivity benefits of AI while the practices to govern and secure these systems are still developing. Security Depends on the Full Agent Stack Applications depend on code, data, identities, services and infrastructure. Security depends on how those components work together — and AI agents extend that system . Models provide capabilities; harnesses organize context, tools and workflows; and runtime environments provide the infrastructure within which actions execute. Each part of that stack carries security responsibilities, and proper protection requires controls across each layer, as data, instructions and actions move through the system. Consider an agent updating a customer record. Say it encounters malicious instructions in an attached document and attempts to export customer data to an unauthorized destination.
